query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Dynamic recrystallization induced by severe plastic deformation refines the grain structure of high-entropy alloys, and this grain refinement governs the increase in hardness and strength via the Hall–Petch mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast high-entropy alloy with a mixed-phase microstructure (e.g., coarse FCC/BCC or similar phases typical of the cast state)
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a severe plastic deformation process (e.g., additive friction stir deposition, AFSD) designed to induce dynamic recrystallization
generation.conditions: Keep the alloy composition and overall processing environment constant; only vary the processing method between as-cast and thermomechanically processed states under comparable strain rates and controlled processing temperatures that promote DRX without causing additional phase formation or excessive thermal degradation
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size reduction (nanocrystalline or near-nanocrystalline structure) achieved by dynamic recrystallization
generation.mechanism: The refined grains produce a higher density of grain boundaries which act as barriers to dislocation movement, thereby increasing hardness and yield/ultimate strength following a Hall–Petch type relationship
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline as-cast material, the AFSD-processed high-entropy alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and strength, with measurable reductions in average grain size correlating with the improvements
generation.baseline: As-cast high-entropy alloy with coarser grain structure and the typical mechanical properties expected for its phase composition
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for high-entropy alloys where microstructure is initially coarse and where processing conditions are sufficient to trigger significant dynamic recrystallization without promoting unwanted phase changes. Its applicability may be limited when the alloy composition strongly favors extremely stable phases or when processing conditions lead to excessive thermal exposure that causes grain growth or phase decomposition
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of strengthening, including trade-offs in ductility, and the sensitivity to specific processing parameters remains to be quantified; there is also some uncertainty if additional mechanisms (e.g., precipitation hardening) play a significant role in some HEA systems

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same high-entropy alloy: one in the as-cast state and one processed by AFSD under controlled conditions. Characterize the microstructure via electron microscopy (to measure grain size) and determine phase composition by X-ray diffraction. Measure hardness (using microindentation or nanoindentation) and yield/ultimate strength (via compression or tensile testing). Correlate the mechanical property improvements with grain size reduction.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate strength (from mechanical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AFSD-processed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in grain size compared to the as-cast samples, or if the observed hardness and strength do not improve in accordance with the Hall–Petch relationship (i.e., if no correlation between grain refinement and increased properties is evident), then the hypothesis that DRX-induced grain refinement governs hardness and strength would be falsified

However, many of the investigated alloys contained more than just FCC and BCC phases. Currently, there is limited work on how these solid solution materials behave under various processes that change the established cast microstructure, with most of the work on the additive space, focusing on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) or directed energy deposition (DED) [,,,,].
